# Native Advertising and Sponsored Content Explained

Source: https://lowob.com/research/native-advertising-and-sponsored-content/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-06 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Native advertising is paid placement that matches the form of the content around it; sponsored content is the subset where the advertiser supplies or commissions an actual piece. Both suit products that need explaining, but disclosure is not optional: the FTC, the EU's Unfair Commercial Practices Directive and the UK's ASA all require paid content to be clearly identifiable, and the advertiser is responsible alongside the publisher.

Native advertising is paid placement designed to match the form and function of the content around it. Sponsored content is the subset where the advertiser supplies or commissions an actual piece, published by a third party with a paid label. Both exist because conventional ad formats are ignored, and both carry a risk conventional ads do not: being mistaken for editorial. In one University of Georgia study only 7% of readers identified a sponsored article as advertising. Disclosure is not optional, the advertiser is responsible alongside the publisher, and the format works best for products that need explaining.

Native advertising takes many forms: a promoted article in a publication's feed, a recommended story at the end of a news piece, a sponsored post in a social feed, a paid segment in a newsletter. What they share is that the reader meets them in a mode of attention rather than avoidance.

## The main forms

| Form | How it is bought | Strength | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| In-feed native units | Programmatically or directly, on social platforms and publisher sites; look like posts or articles and lead to the advertiser's page | Scale, targeting | Low-quality placements if bought on defaults |
| Content recommendation placements | Through networks that place "you may also like" modules across many publishers | Cheap, broad | Variable quality; headings that look editorial |
| Sponsored articles and videos | From a publication, newsletter or creator, produced by the publisher's studio or supplied by the advertiser | Room to explain | Being mistaken for editorial |
| Newsletter and podcast sponsorships | The host reads or writes about the sponsor in their own voice | The host's trust transfers | Claims the host cannot substantiate |

Newsletter and podcast sponsorships are among the most effective forms for considered products, because the trust of the host transfers. Our piece on [sponsorships, events, newsletters and podcasts](https://lowob.com/research/sponsorships-events-newsletters-podcasts/) covers how to price and evaluate them.

## Why they work when they work

They meet the reader in a mode of attention rather than avoidance. A reader of a personal-finance newsletter who encounters a sponsored explanation of a product, in the newsletter's voice, with the publisher's implicit endorsement, is more receptive than the same reader seeing a banner. For products that need explaining, which describes most fintech, AI and Web3 products, the format allows explanation.

The same quality is the risk. Wojdynski and Evans's experiments at the University of Georgia, published in the Journal of Advertising in 2015, found that in one study only 17 of 242 readers (7%) identified a sponsored article as advertising, and in an eye-tracking study 17% did. Readers were about seven times more likely to recognise the ad when it was labelled "advertising" or "sponsored content" than when it was labelled "brand voice" or "presented by". A format that persuades because it resembles editorial will mislead unless the label does real work.

## Where the line is

Disclosure is not optional. Regulators in the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom and elsewhere require that paid content be clearly identified as such, in a way the reader will notice before or as they engage with it.

| Jurisdiction | Rule | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| United States | FTC Enforcement Policy Statement and business guide on native advertising, December 2015 | Ads must be identifiable before the reader reaches the main advertising page; labels go immediately in front of or above the headline |
| European Union | Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, Annex I, point 11 | Using paid editorial content to promote a product without making that clear is banned in all circumstances |
| United Kingdom | CAP Code section 2, applied by the ASA | Marketing must be obviously identifiable; the ASA suggests labels such as "ad", "paid-for ad" or "ad link" near recommendation headings |

The FTC's guidance is the most specific. It names "Ad", "Advertisement", "Paid Advertisement" and "Sponsored Advertising Content" as labels likely to be understood. It warns that "Promoted" and "Promoted Stories" are ambiguous, because they may suggest the publisher endorses the content. It says "Sponsored by [X]", "Presented by [X]" and "Brought to you by [X]" may be read as meaning the sponsor paid for the content but did not create or influence it, which is misleading when the sponsor wrote it. And it says a disclosure placed below or to the right of the headline is less likely to be seen. A small grey "Promoted" on the far side of the page fails on both counts.

The ASA has applied the same logic. It found a "Recommended by" footer and the heading "You may also like these" insufficient on a content recommendation widget, and in October 2026 ruled that a footer disclaimer labelling a page as advertorial did not make the ads obviously identifiable.

The advertiser is responsible alongside the publisher. The FTC's guide addresses advertisers directly and says everyone involved in creating or presenting native ads, including agencies and affiliate networks, should make sure they do not mislead about their commercial nature.

> A format that persuades because it resembles editorial will mislead unless the label does real work.

Beyond the legal line is a reputational one. Sponsored content that pretends to be independent, or that makes claims the publisher would never make editorially, damages both parties when discovered, and it is discovered.

## How to buy it well

1. **Choose publishers whose readers are the buyer,** not whose traffic is large.
2. **Brief for a job, not a talking point:** the reader's question, the product truth, what may not be said. Our piece on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) sets out a one-page brief that works for sponsored pieces as well as owned ones.
3. **Let the publisher write in their voice.** Content that reads like the advertiser's brochure fails.
4. **Insist on the disclosure the law requires and make it visible:** a clear word such as "Advertisement", above the headline, on every device and in shared links.
5. **Track with a dedicated link or code.**
6. **Measure comprehension and action, not impressions.**
7. **In reviewed categories, apply the same claims library that governs the ads,** because the publisher's lawyers will ask for it and the regulator will not distinguish.

The best sponsored pieces carry an argument the advertiser could also use in a sales conversation. Our piece on [thought leadership that sales can use](https://lowob.com/research/thought-leadership-that-sales-can-use/) shows how one position can become a diagnostic, a business case and an objection answer, which is the raw material a publisher's studio needs.

## For companies the platforms restrict

Native and sponsored placements are often available to categories the large ad platforms refuse, because the decision is the publisher's rather than a classifier's. A publication that covers personal finance will run a compliant sponsored explanation of a savings product; a platform's automated review may not. That makes the format part of the open band for many restricted businesses, and one of the few that allows the full explanation the product needs. Our piece on [distribution when ad platforms restrict you](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) places native alongside the other open-band channels.

## lowob takeaways

- **Native fits its surroundings.** That is why it works and why it can mislead.
- **Use a plain label.** "Ad" or "Advertisement", above the headline; avoid "Promoted".
- **The advertiser is responsible too.** FTC, EU and UK rules do not leave it to the publisher.
- **Brief for the reader's question.** Let the publisher's voice carry the explanation.
- **Measure action.** Dedicated links or codes, not impressions.

## Sources and notes

- [FTC, Native Advertising: A Guide for Businesses](https://ftc.gov/tips-advice/business-center/guidance/native-advertising-guide-businesses), December 2015. US regulator guidance; companion to the Enforcement Policy Statement on deceptively formatted advertisements.
- [legislation.gov.uk, Directive 2005/29/EC (Unfair Commercial Practices Directive), Annex I](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2005/29/annex/I/adopted), as adopted. EU law; check member state implementation and later amendments.
- [ASA, Recognising ads: native advertising](https://www.asa.org.uk/advice-online/recognising-ads-native-advertising.html), updated 23 October 2026. UK self-regulatory advice; not a statute.
- [University of Georgia, Despite growth, native advertising is still difficult for consumers to recognize](https://news.uga.edu/native-advertising-research-2015/), 16 December 2015. University summary of a peer-reviewed study; small samples, older formats.

## Next move

Look at your last three sponsored placements as a reader would. If the label is anything other than a plain "Ad" or "Advertisement" above the headline, ask the publisher to change it, and brief the next piece around one question your buyer actually asks.
